headings.title: Understanding Drug Over-Prescription and the National Drug Policy
headings.content: Drug over-prescription occurs when healthcare providers write medication orders that are clinically unnecessary, excessive in dosage, or continued past the appropriate therapeutic window. In clinical practice, this practice wastes scarce resources and directly harms patients. Nigeria's **National Drug Policy** provides the regulatory framework designed to ensure that medicines available to the public are safe, effective, and of good quality. It guides how drugs are manufactured, imported, distributed, and prescribed across all levels of care. Despite these guidelines, weak enforcement and patient pressure often lead to rampant misuse. Nurses play a crucial frontline role in identifying inappropriate drug orders before they reach the patient, acting as a vital safety net in both primary health centres and large teaching hospitals.

headings.title: Drivers of Inappropriate Prescribing: Behavioral and Systemic Factors
headings.content: Multiple pressures push clinicians to write unneeded prescriptions. Patients often equate good medical care with receiving a physical product, leading them to demand antibiotics for viral infections or strong analgesics for minor discomforts. Clinicians may yield to these demands simply to shorten consultation times. On the systemic side, aggressive pharmaceutical marketing and financial incentives can heavily bias prescribing habits. A common misconception in busy outpatient clinics is that adding a new drug is always safer than withholding treatment or waiting to see if symptoms resolve on their own.

headings.title: Common Forms of Polypharmacy and Inappropriate Regimens
headings.content:
Inappropriate prescribing manifests in several distinct ways that clinical nurses must recognize during medication administration rounds.

- **Polypharmacy**: The simultaneous use of multiple medications by a patient, often defined as taking five or more daily drugs, which exponentially increases adverse drug events.
- **Prescribing Cascades**: A phenomenon where an adverse drug reaction is misinterpreted as a new medical condition, leading to the addition of yet another unnecessary drug.
- **Oversupplication**: Giving excessive quantities of a drug for a short-term ailment, leaving dangerous leftover medications in home environments.
- **Therapeutic Duplication**: Prescribing two or more drugs from the same pharmacological class without clinical justification, such as two different NSAIDs.

headings.title: Consequences on Patient Safety and Public Health
headings.content: The fallout from over-prescribing extends far beyond individual inconvenience. Patients face severe adverse drug reactions, toxic drug-drug interactions, and increased rates of accidental overdoses, particularly among elderly populations with declining renal and hepatic clearance. From a broader public health perspective, the indiscriminate use of antibiotics drives the global crisis of antimicrobial resistance, rendering routine infections potentially untreatable. Furthermore, financial toxicity forces families to deplete household savings on unnecessary pharmaceutical items, compromising spending on basic nutritional needs.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Medication Review
headings.content: Nurses occupy an ideal position to conduct systematic medication reviews during admission, ward rounds, and discharge planning. The assessment process involves cross-checking every prescribed item against the patient's current clinical diagnosis, laboratory values, and actual complaints. Nurses look out for red flags such as duplicate therapies, prolonged courses of proton pump inhibitors without clear indications, or sedatives continued long-term. Involving the patient and their caregivers in this review helps uncover self-medication habits, herbal supplement use, and confusion over complex dosing schedules.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions for Rational Prescribing
headings.content: Combatting over-prescription requires proactive nursing strategies. Nurses can advocate for patients during multidisciplinary team meetings, questioning questionable orders respectfully and offering evidence-based alternatives. Patient education is equally powerful; nurses must explain why a particular drug is unnecessary, helping to manage expectations and reduce the demand for quick-fix pills. Additionally, implementing structured bedside reconciliation protocols ensures that discrepancies introduced during patient transfers between wards are swiftly corrected.

headings.title: Regulatory Strategies and Policy Enforcement
headings.content: Addressing systemic over-prescription requires robust regulatory oversight by bodies such as the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) and the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria (PCN). These agencies enforce regulations on drug promotion, monitor distribution channels, and crack down on patent medicine vendors who dispense prescription-only drugs without authorization. Institutional policies, such as mandatory antibiotic stewardship programs and regular drug audits in hospitals, reinforce these national laws. Strengthening compliance ensures that medicines are dispensed only when clinically warranted, protecting both vulnerable patients and public health.
